requirements.requirement: New user passwords must be at least 12 characters long on node1
requirements.summary: A libpwquality drop-in (/etc/security/pwquality.conf.d/90-antrieb-policy.conf) sets minlen=12, wired through existing pam_pwquality entries in system-auth/password-auth. Verified directly: pwscore rejected a 7-char password citing 'shorter than 12 characters' (cmd-fbbdb07429914818), and a real PAM-driven passwd flow rejected a 7-char password (cmd-d0affc3139394c58) while accepting a 14-char compliant password (cmd-12ffc078eba24411). Config and enforcement persisted after reboot (cmd-98e4426ad46e45af, cmd-370084b59be34af3).

requirements.requirement: New user passwords must use at least three different character classes on node1
requirements.summary: Same drop-in sets minclass=3. pwscore directly rejected a lowercase-only password ('less than 3 character classes', cmd-61dfd53213204e3a). A real PAM passwd flow rejected a 16-char two-class password (cmd-a67f0c82849c4d8d) and accepted a 14-char three-class password (cmd-12ffc078eba24411). Re-verified after reboot with a fresh test user (cmd-370084b59be34af3).

requirements.requirement: Policy applies to new user password changes via the actual PAM stack, not just a standalone checker
requirements.summary: Beyond pwscore (a standalone quality checker), the executor created real test users and drove password changes through the actual passwd/PAM pipeline (pam_pwquality already present in system-auth and password-auth per cmd-30bc22fb8a534204), confirming enforcement at the point new user passwords are actually set, both before and after reboot.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on node1 (pre-restart baseline, restart ack, changed boot identity, recovered service/config state)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured boot_id 31b01b46..., uptime, policy file, and sshd active (cmd-28dcbd20e2cc4d9b). A backgrounded reboot returned its ack before disconnection (cmd-50f2be1c399b4d94). Exec briefly failed mid-reboot (cmd-9c847827a63a46dc) then succeeded (cmd-e1aec9529fb84430), and boot_id/uptime changed to 073a2c3c.../22:56:30 (cmd-98e4426ad46e45af), consistent with the fixed after_executor lifecycle snapshot. Policy file and sshd active were reconfirmed post-restart, and a fresh end-to-end PAM enforcement test was re-run successfully (cmd-370084b59be34af3).

overall_summary: The password complexity policy (minlen=12, minclass=3) was correctly configured via a pwquality.conf.d drop-in on node1 and verified both by pwscore and, more rigorously, by real end-to-end PAM/passwd flows with disposable test users — confirming rejection of short and low-class passwords and acceptance of compliant ones. The mandatory node-restart evidence protocol was fully and directly observed: pre-restart baseline, an acknowledged reboot, a confirmed change in boot identity consistent with the fixed lifecycle snapshots, and full post-restart recovery of the policy file, sshd, and PAM enforcement. The only hygiene concern is an unremoved timestamped backup of the original pwquality.conf created defensively before writing the drop-in; it is bounded and low-risk but was not shown to be cleaned up.
limitations: The unconditional backup file created by cmd-2cd221be99ed4094 (/etc/security/pwquality.conf.bak.<timestamp>) is not covered by the fixed lifecycle snapshots (which only inventory /tmp), so its final disposition (retained vs. later removed) cannot be independently confirmed.
Evidence relies on command stdout captured by the executor rather than independent verifier access; all conclusions are drawn solely from the reported transcript and fixed snapshots.

operational_hygiene.summary: Reviewed all state-changing commands: creation of the pwquality drop-in (cmd-2cd221be99ed4094) directly serves the task outcome; test users pwpolicytest/pwpolicytest2 were created for enforcement verification and both were cleaned up, including a follow-up pkill+userdel after the first userdel failed due to a lingering login process (cmd-e62aa2ddd80f4485, cmd-13b4510d13054cde, cmd-0abb7440b01d4fb5) — a legitimate corrective action, not a new mutation. The reboot itself was a required part of the mandated restart protocol and produced only an incidental /tmp/reboot.log, a bounded low-risk artifact. One unnecessary residue: cmd-2cd221be99ed4094 unconditionally created a timestamped backup copy of /etc/security/pwquality.conf (a defensive habit with no described rollback need for a drop-in file added under pwquality.conf.d/) that was never explicitly removed; this file is outside the /tmp inventory captured by the lifecycle snapshots so its continued presence cannot be independently confirmed either way. No failed services, no exposed sockets beyond the pre-existing sshd, and package-health manager check remained unchanged across snapshots.
